Once, when the great sage Valmiki was seated in his ashram, the divine sage Narada came to visit him. Valmiki welcomed him warmly and asked who, in the present age, was a man endowed with virtue, strength, righteousness, gratitude, truthfulness, firm vows, good conduct, goodwill toward all beings, learning, capability, a pleasing appearance, self-control, mastery over anger, and the power to strike fear into gods and demons alike in battle. Narada replied that such a combination of qualities was rare to find, but that Shri Rama, son of King Dasharatha of the Ikshvaku dynasty, possessed all these virtues. Narada then recounted to Valmiki a brief account of Shri Rama's life, covering the events from his birth up to his coronation.

After Narada departed, one day Valmiki went with his disciple Bharadwaja to bathe on the banks of the Tamasa river. There he saw a pair of krauncha birds affectionately courting each other. Suddenly a hunter shot an arrow and killed the male krauncha, which fell writhing to the ground. Its mate began to wail in grief. Moved by compassion at this pitiful sight, a verse spontaneously rose to Valmiki's lips, in which he cursed the hunter to never find peace for having killed one of a pair of birds absorbed in love. This verse was metrical and rhythmic, and is considered to be the first shloka ever composed.

When he returned to his ashram and was still reflecting on this event, Brahma himself appeared before Valmiki. Valmiki worshipped him with reverence. Brahma told him that the verse that had come from his lips had done so by Brahma's own will, and that he should now compose the entire story of Shri Rama in that same meter. Brahma granted him the boon that the complete story of Rama, including its hidden aspects, would become known to him spontaneously, and that untruth would never enter his composition. Thus, on Brahma's command, Valmiki began composing the Ramayana.

The story begins with a description of Ayodhya, the capital of the Kosala kingdom. Situated on the banks of the river Sarayu, this city was extremely prosperous, vast, and beautiful. Its main roads were wide and well laid out, its houses tall and magnificent, and the city never lacked for grain or water. Ayodhya was home to warriors skilled in the art of weaponry, brahmins learned in the Vedas, and a righteous populace. This city was ruled by the kings of the Surya dynasty, founded by King Ikshvaku. Many illustrious kings were born in this line, among them King Dasharatha.

King Dasharatha was righteous, devoted to his subjects, and valiant. He had three queens - Kaushalya, Sumitra, and Kaikeyi. Though King Dasharatha possessed every kind of wealth, he remained constantly troubled because he had no children. Needing a son to carry on his lineage, he decided, on the advice of his family priest Vashishtha, to perform the Ashvamedha sacrifice. Preparations for this sacrifice began.

At that time, minister Sumantra told King Dasharatha the story of the sage Rishyashringa. Rishyashringa was the son of the sage Vibhandaka and, having grown up in the forest from childhood, knew nothing of women. When a drought struck the kingdom of Anga, its King Romapada brought Rishyashringa to his kingdom with the help of courtesans, after which rain fell, and King Romapada gave his daughter Shanta in marriage to Rishyashringa. King Dasharatha went to Romapada and brought Rishyashringa to Ayodhya for his sacrifice.

Under Rishyashringa's supervision, a grand Ashvamedha sacrifice was completed on the northern bank of the Sarayu river. After the sacrifice concluded, Rishyashringa advised King Dasharatha to perform the Putrakameshti sacrifice to obtain sons. This sacrifice too was carried out according to proper rites. During the sacrifice, the gods went to Brahma and expressed their suffering at the hands of Ravana. Ravana had received a boon from Brahma that he could not be killed by gods, demons, gandharvas, or rakshasas, but since he had scorned humans and monkeys as too insignificant to seek protection from, he had not asked for safety from them. So the gods prayed to Lord Vishnu to take a human form and slay Ravana. Lord Vishnu decided to incarnate as the son of King Dasharatha.

From the fire of the Putrakameshti sacrifice, a divine being emerged holding a golden vessel filled with payasam (sacred rice pudding). He told King Dasharatha to distribute this payasam among his queens. King Dasharatha gave half to Kaushalya, and divided the remaining half between Sumitra and Kaikeyi. In due course, on the ninth day of the month of Chaitra, Kaushalya gave birth to Shri Rama, who carried the full radiance of an aspect of Lord Vishnu. Kaikeyi gave birth to Bharata, and Sumitra gave birth to twin sons, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. The birth of the four princes filled Ayodhya with joy.

The four princes grew up under the guidance of their family priest Vashishtha. Lakshmana held special affection for Rama, and Shatrughna for Bharata. All four brothers became accomplished in the Vedas, archery, and the scriptures. Shri Rama excelled in all virtues, and both the people and his father Dasharatha held him in special love.

One day the great sage Vishwamitra came to Ayodhya. He told King Dasharatha that the demons Maricha and Subahu were constantly disrupting his sacrifice and defiling it. He requested that Shri Rama be sent with him to protect the sacrifice. Fearing separation from his son, King Dasharatha was deeply distressed and offered to go himself with his army, but Vishwamitra made it clear that only Shri Rama was capable of this task. Finally, at the persuasion of Guru Vashishtha, King Dasharatha sent Shri Rama and Lakshmana with Vishwamitra.

Along the way, Vishwamitra taught Shri Rama two mystical powers called Bala and Atibala, which would keep him free from fatigue, hunger, and thirst, and would increase his radiance. They then reached the Tadaka forest near the confluence of the Sarayu and Ganga. Vishwamitra told the story of the demoness Tadaka, daughter of the yaksha Suketu and wife of the demon Sunda, who had been turned into a fearsome rakshasi by the curse of the sage Agastya and was laying waste to the forest. On Vishwamitra's instruction, Shri Rama, despite her being a woman, slew Tadaka for the good of the people.

After the slaying of Tadaka, Vishwamitra, pleased, bestowed upon Shri Rama many divine weapons, including the Dandachakra, Dharmachakra, Kalachakra, Vishnuchakra, Aindrastra, Vajrastra, and Shivastra, among many other celestial arms. Along with these, he also taught him the knowledge of how to recall these weapons. They then reached Vishwamitra's ashram, where the sacrifice began. Shri Rama and Lakshmana stayed constantly vigilant to protect the sacrifice. After six days, when Maricha and Subahu came to disrupt the sacrifice, Shri Rama used the Manavastra to hurl Maricha far into the ocean, and slew Subahu with the Agneyastra, destroying the rest of the demons as well. Thus the sacrifice was completed without further disturbance.

After the sacrifice was completed, Vishwamitra decided to take Shri Rama and Lakshmana to the city of Mithila for King Janaka's bow sacrifice. Along the way, he told them the story of the descent of the Ganga. In ancient times, King Sagara of Ayodhya had performed an Ashvamedha sacrifice, in which his sixty thousand sons guarded the sacrificial horse. Indra stole the horse and tied it up in the ashram of the sage Kapila. Sagara's sons accused Kapila of theft, and enraged, Kapila reduced all those sons to ashes with the power of his austerities. To liberate these sons, the descent of the Ganga was necessary, so that her sacred waters could touch their ashes and grant them heaven.

Sagara's descendant Bhagiratha undertook severe penance for this purpose. Pleased with his penance, Brahma granted the boon that Ganga would descend to earth, but since the earth could not withstand the tremendous force of Ganga's descent, Lord Shiva agreed to receive Ganga in his matted locks. Pleased by Bhagiratha's penance, Shiva absorbed Ganga into his locks and then gradually released her onto the earth. Ganga followed behind Bhagiratha's chariot and eventually reached the ocean, where she purified the ashes of Sagara's sons, granting them heaven. For this reason, Ganga is also called Bhagirathi.

Continuing their journey, they reached the ashram of the sage Gautama, where Vishwamitra told the story of Ahalya. Gautama's wife Ahalya was extremely beautiful. Once, Indra deceitfully took the form of Gautama and united with Ahalya. When Gautama returned and learned of this deception, he angrily cursed Indra, and also cursed Ahalya to remain in the ashram without air or food, invisible, performing penance, until the dust of Shri Rama's feet touched her, only then would she be freed. Years later, when Shri Rama entered that ashram and touched the ground with his feet, Ahalya was released from the curse and appeared in her original divine form. Gautama also came there and took his wife back.

Thereafter, Vishwamitra, Shri Rama, and Lakshmana reached the city of Mithila. King Janaka of Mithila was a great ruler of the Videha dynasty, himself supremely wise and righteous. He had a daughter named Sita, whose birth had been extraordinary. Once, while ploughing the sacrificial ground, a girl had emerged from the earth at the tip of the plough, whom King Janaka adopted as his daughter and named Sita, since sita means the furrow made by a plough. As Sita grew up, she became an exceptionally beautiful, virtuous, and radiant young woman.

King Janaka possessed a divine bow of Lord Shiva, which had come to him through tradition. This bow was so heavy and powerful that lifting it was impossible for an ordinary man. King Janaka had decreed that whichever man could lift this bow and string it would be married to Sita. Many kings and princes had tried, but none could even move the bow.

Vishwamitra brought Shri Rama and Lakshmana to King Janaka's court. King Janaka welcomed them grandly and told them the story of the bow. On Vishwamitra's instruction, Shri Rama approached the massive bow. He lifted it with ease, and as he tried to string it, the mighty bow broke in the middle with a sound like a terrible roar. Witnessing this, everyone present was astonished. King Janaka, overjoyed, declared in keeping with his vow that Sita would be married to Shri Rama, and sent word to Ayodhya.

Upon receiving the news, King Dasharatha, along with Guru Vashishtha, other sages, and his family, came to Mithila. The two kings together made arrangements for the wedding. On this occasion, it was decided that not only Shri Rama and Sita, but all four brothers would be married. King Janaka's younger brother Kushadhwaja had two daughters, Mandavi and Shrutakirti, while Sita's younger sister was Urmila. In accordance with proper rites, Shri Rama was married to Sita, Lakshmana to Urmila, Bharata to Mandavi, and Shatrughna to Shrutakirti. A festive atmosphere filled all of Mithila and Ayodhya.

After the wedding, as everyone was returning to Ayodhya, a fearsome event occurred along the way. The great sage Parashurama, who had rid the earth of kshatriyas twenty-one times, arrived in an enraged state. He had heard news of the breaking of Shiva's bow, which was very dear to him. He stopped King Dasharatha's procession and issued a challenge, asking Shri Rama to string the bow of Vishnu that he carried, so that his valor could be tested. King Dasharatha grew fearful, but Shri Rama humbly stepped forward, took the bow from Parashurama's hands, and effortlessly strung an arrow upon it.

Seeing this, Parashurama's radiance began to fade, and he realized that Shri Rama was none other than an incarnation of Vishnu himself. He told Shri Rama that his arrow must either destroy his own power of movement or the worlds he had attained through his austerities, since it could not be withdrawn without effect. Shri Rama chose to destroy the worlds gained through his austerities, which completely humbled Parashurama's pride. Accepting his defeat, Parashurama went off to perform penance on Mount Mahendra.

After this event, King Dasharatha, his four sons, and their new brides, along with the entire procession, reached Ayodhya peacefully. The city gave them a grand welcome, and an atmosphere of joy and celebration prevailed everywhere. Shri Rama lived happily with Sita in the palace of Ayodhya, and thus concludes the story of the Bala Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, which describes all the major events from Shri Rama's birth through his marriage and return to Ayodhya.

After Shri Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana returned to Ayodhya following the weddings of all four brothers, a long period of happiness, peace, and prosperity prevailed in Ayodhya. King Dasharatha had now grown old, and he began to feel that his life would not be long. He had a single wish in his heart: to crown his eldest son Shri Rama as crown prince while he was still alive, so that the burden of the kingdom would pass into capable hands. Shri Rama was foremost in all virtues, devoted to his subjects, righteous, and deeply loved by the entire populace of Ayodhya as well as by the ministers.

One day King Dasharatha gathered all his ministers, feudal lords, priests, and representatives of the people in his royal court. He spoke of his age and his reign, and declared that he now wished to crown his eldest son Shri Rama as crown prince. Everyone present in the assembly joyfully welcomed this proposal and unanimously gave their consent to Shri Rama's coronation. King Dasharatha immediately ordered Guru Vashishtha and the other priests to begin preparations for the coronation, and it was decided that the ceremony would take place the very next day under the Pushya constellation.

Upon hearing this news, a wave of joy swept through the whole city of Ayodhya. Decorative arches were raised at every home, roads were cleaned, the city was adorned with flags and banners, and the people enthusiastically prepared for the coronation. King Dasharatha called Shri Rama to inform him of this decision and asked him to observe a fast and keep the required vows. Shri Rama, obeying his father's command, observed the fast along with Sita.

But amid this joyful atmosphere, a wicked conspiracy was about to begin. Kaikeyi's maidservant Manthara, who was hunchbacked and of a crooked nature, was watching the city's decorations and festivities from the palace terrace. When she learned that all this excitement was because of Shri Rama's coronation, jealousy and malice flared up in her heart. She immediately went to Kaikeyi and told her the news, saying that instead of being a happy occasion, this was in fact a terrible day for Kaikeyi, because if Shri Rama became king, then Kaikeyi and her son Bharata would become entirely secondary, while Kaushalya's status would rise.

At first Kaikeyi was pleased to hear this, since she regarded Shri Rama as her own son, and she gave Manthara a valuable ornament as a gift for this good news. But Manthara cleverly continued to plant doubt and fear in Kaikeyi's mind. She reminded Kaikeyi that Bharata was currently away at his maternal grandfather's kingdom of Kekaya, and that if Shri Rama became king, Bharata would have no place in the future, and would instead have to obey Shri Rama's commands or might even be exiled. Manthara used Kaikeyi's maternal affection and love for her son to gradually incite her.

Manthara reminded Kaikeyi that in the past, during the war between the gods and demons, when King Dasharatha was wounded in battle, Kaikeyi herself had driven his chariot and saved his life. Pleased at the time, King Dasharatha had asked Kaikeyi to request two boons, but Kaikeyi had not asked for them then, saying she would ask later. Manthara advised Kaikeyi that now was the time to use those two boons - one to demand the throne for Bharata, and the other to send Shri Rama into exile in the forest for fourteen years. Under Manthara's wicked counsel, Kaikeyi's mind gradually began to waver, and eventually she was persuaded by her words.

On Manthara's advice, Kaikeyi removed her jewelry, put on plain clothes, and went to lie on the floor of the chamber of anger, as though deeply grieved and furious. When King Dasharatha came to see his beloved queen Kaikeyi and found her in this state, he was greatly distressed and asked the reason. He tried to console her lovingly and promised that he would grant whatever she asked, and even swore an oath to that effect. Hearing this, Kaikeyi presented her demand and reminded King Dasharatha of his two old promised boons.

Kaikeyi clearly demanded that in the first boon, Bharata be crowned king, and in the second boon, Shri Rama be sent into exile in the Dandaka forest for fourteen years. Hearing this, King Dasharatha felt as though struck by a thunderbolt, and he fainted. When he regained consciousness, he tried in many ways to persuade, plead with, and threaten Kaikeyi, but Kaikeyi remained firm in her resolve and repeatedly reminded her truthful husband to keep his word. King Dasharatha suffered through the entire night in grief and anguish, his body becoming lifeless with sorrow.

In the morning, when Shri Rama learned of his father's condition, he went immediately to Kaikeyi. Kaikeyi herself told Shri Rama the entire matter and asked him to honor his father's word. Shri Rama, without the slightest hesitation, gladly accepted this command. He told Kaikeyi that he was ready to go to the forest at once to fulfill his father's promise, and that he had no objection to Bharata's coronation. There was neither anger nor sorrow in his heart; rather, he considered upholding righteousness and his father's word to be his highest duty.

Shri Rama then went to his mother Kaushalya and told her the news. Kaushalya was deeply grieved to hear this and began to lament, but Shri Rama consoled her and explained the importance of patience and righteousness. Lakshmana was present there and felt intense anger toward Kaikeyi and the entire situation. He even spoke of taking up arms in protest, but Shri Rama calmed him and explained the importance of obeying their father's command and upholding righteousness, after which Lakshmana calmed down and firmly resolved to go to the forest with Shri Rama.

When Sita learned this news, she too firmly resolved to go to the forest with her husband. At first Shri Rama tried to persuade Sita to remain in Ayodhya by describing the hardships of forest life, wild animals, and difficulties, but Sita, upholding her duty as a devoted wife, clearly said that without her husband, even the palace of Ayodhya would be like exile to her, and that the forest with her husband would be like heaven. Eventually, seeing Sita's determination, Shri Rama agreed to take her along.

When the people of Ayodhya learned that their beloved Shri Rama was being sent into exile, an atmosphere of grief spread throughout the city. People grew angry at Kaikeyi and began pleading with Shri Rama to stop, but Shri Rama remained firm in his decision. Shri Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana put on simple bark garments and took their final blessing from King Dasharatha. King Dasharatha was utterly devastated at the mere thought of separation from his son, and bidding farewell to Shri Rama became unbearable for him.

All the people of Ayodhya, including women, men, the elderly, and children, began following behind Shri Rama's chariot, weeping and pleading for them to return. Minister Sumantra was driving the chariot. During the night, when the people of Ayodhya fell asleep from exhaustion, Shri Rama asked Sumantra to drive the chariot forward quickly, so that the people could not follow them and would return to their homes.

On the first night, they stopped on the banks of the Tamasa river. The next morning, when they moved forward, they found that the people of Ayodhya were still following them. Shri Rama cleverly slipped away under cover of darkness during the night, leaving the people behind so that they would return home. They then reached Shringaverapura on the banks of the Ganga, the kingdom of the Nishada king Guha. Guha was a close friend of Shri Rama and welcomed him with great respect, offering all manner of hospitality, but Shri Rama, following the vow of forest life, accepted only simple food and rest beneath a tree.

The next day, Lakshmana matted his hair, and with Guha's help, they crossed the Ganga and reached the ashram of the sage Bharadwaja at Prayaga. Bharadwaja welcomed them and advised them to settle at Mount Chitrakuta, a beautiful and peaceful place with ample fruits, flowers, and water. Following Bharadwaja's advice, Shri Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana proceeded to Mount Chitrakuta and built a beautiful hut of leaves to live in.

Meanwhile, Sumantra returned to Ayodhya with the empty chariot. His return brought a wave of grief over Ayodhya. King Dasharatha was completely broken by the sorrow of separation from his son. He recalled an incident from his youth, when he had unknowingly killed a young man named Shravana Kumar, the son of blind parents, and at that time Shravana's father had cursed him that he too would die in separation from his son. Remembering this curse and pining in separation from Shri Rama, King Dasharatha finally gave up his life.

At that time, Bharata and Shatrughna were at their maternal grandfather's kingdom of Kekaya. The ministers urgently summoned them to Ayodhya, but they were not told anything about King Dasharatha's death or Shri Rama's exile. Upon reaching Ayodhya, Bharata was astonished to see the atmosphere of grief in the city. When he went to his mother Kaikeyi, she proudly told him the whole story of how she had demanded the throne for Bharata and exile for Shri Rama.

Hearing this, Bharata was extremely angry and grieved. He harshly reproached his mother Kaikeyi and condemned her wicked act. He clearly said that he did not want a kingdom obtained through his mother's deceit. Bharata also held Manthara responsible as the root cause of this entire conspiracy and expressed great anger toward her. Bharata then performed his father's final funeral rites and paid his respects.

The ministers and Guru Vashishtha urged Bharata to take the throne, but Bharata clearly refused. He said that the rightful ruler of Ayodhya was Shri Rama alone, and that he himself would go to Chitrakuta to bring Shri Rama back to Ayodhya. With this resolve, Bharata set out for Chitrakuta with a vast army, the queen mothers, Guru Vashishtha, and the people. Along the way, they reached the ashram of the sage Bharadwaja, who received them with hospitality and showed them the way to Chitrakuta.

When Bharata reached Chitrakuta and saw Shri Rama living a simple life in bark garments, his heart was overwhelmed, and he fell at Shri Rama's feet in deep emotion. Shri Rama also embraced Bharata with love. Bharata gave Shri Rama the news of their father's death, which grieved Shri Rama greatly, and he offered water oblations to his father with the waters of the Ganga.

Bharata then requested Shri Rama to return to Ayodhya and take up the burden of the kingdom. He said that he did not want the kingdom obtained through his mother's act, and that Shri Rama alone was the rightful heir. But Shri Rama firmly said that he was bound to honor his father's word and would not return to Ayodhya without completing fourteen years. He explained to Bharata that upholding his father's promise was his highest duty.

At this time, a sage named Jabali, who held atheistic views, tried to convince Shri Rama through logical arguments that there was no need to be bound by his father's word or by righteousness, and that he should return to Ayodhya and take up the kingdom. Shri Rama gave a fitting reply to Jabali's arguments, saying that the existence of the world is sustained only through truth and righteousness, and that he would never abandon his father's word.

Guru Vashishtha then also gave his own counsel, explaining at length the tradition of the Raghu dynasty, righteousness, and the importance of royal duty, but Shri Rama remained firm in his decision. Finally, when Bharata realized that Shri Rama would not change his decision under any circumstances, he asked Shri Rama for his sandals, so that he could place them on the throne and govern the kingdom as Shri Rama's representative.

Shri Rama accepted Bharata's request and gave him his sandals. Bharata, deeply moved, placed the sandals upon his head and returned to Ayodhya. But Bharata refused to live in the royal palace of Ayodhya and decided to live in a simple hut at a place called Nandigrama. He installed Shri Rama's sandals upon the throne and decided to govern the kingdom for fourteen years as a servant and representative, in the guise of an ascetic, vowing that if Shri Rama did not return after the fourteen years were complete, he would enter fire and give up his body.

Thus Bharata governed the kingdom of the sandals from Nandigrama, while Shri Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana continued their forest life at Chitrakuta, remaining firm in upholding righteousness and their father's word. Thus concludes the story of the Ayodhya Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, which describes all the major events from the preparations for the coronation through Shri Rama's exile, King Dasharatha's death, and the establishment of the rule of the sandals by Bharata.

After the meeting with Bharata at Chitrakuta and his return to Ayodhya, Shri Rama felt that Chitrakuta had now become too well known a place, one which the people of Ayodhya could visit often for his darshan. So he decided to go deeper into the forest. Shri Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana left Chitrakuta and proceeded toward the Dandaka forest. Along the way, they met the great sage Atri and his wife Anasuya. Anasuya instructed Sita on the duties of a devoted wife and gave her divine garments and ornaments as gifts. After taking the blessings of the sage Atri, the three of them entered the Dandaka forest.

In the Dandaka forest, they encountered a fearsome demon named Viradha, who attempted to abduct Sita. Shri Rama and Lakshmana fought him and defeated him, burying him in a pit to kill him. Before dying, Viradha revealed that he had once been a gandharva named Tumburu and had become a demon due to a curse, and that he was liberated by dying at Shri Rama's hands. They then reached the ashram of the sage Sharabhanga, where Sharabhanga gave up his body in fire and attained the world of Brahma. The other sages present there requested Shri Rama to protect them from the torment of demons, and Shri Rama promised them that he would destroy the demons.

They then went to the ashram of the sage Sutikshna, where they stayed for a while. From there they went to the ashram of Agastya's brother, and then to the ashram of the sage Agastya himself. Agastya welcomed Shri Rama warmly and gave him a divine bow, an inexhaustible quiver, and a sword as gifts. On Agastya's advice, Shri Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana went to live at a place called Panchavati, a beautiful spot on the banks of the river Godavari.

At Panchavati, they met Jatayu, a giant vulture-king who was a friend of King Dasharatha. Jatayu promised Shri Rama that he would protect Sita in his absence. Lakshmana built a beautiful hut of leaves at Panchavati, and the three lived there happily.

One day Ravana's sister Shurpanakha came to Panchavati and became infatuated with Shri Rama upon seeing him. She proposed marriage to Shri Rama, but he politely declined and sent her to Lakshmana. Lakshmana also rejected her proposal. Enraged, Shurpanakha tried to attack Sita, at which Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears. In this disfigured state, Shurpanakha went to her brother Khara, who was the demon commander of Janasthana.

Enraged, Khara sent fourteen demons to kill Shri Rama, but Shri Rama single-handedly destroyed them all. Then Khara himself came to fight with an army of fourteen thousand demons, along with his brother Dushana and commander Trishira. Shri Rama single-handedly destroyed this entire army and also killed Khara, Dushana, and Trishira. Hearing this news, Shurpanakha went to Lanka and told Ravana the entire story, along with describing Sita's extraordinary beauty, which awakened in Ravana's mind a desire to possess her.

Ravana went to his uncle Maricha for help. Maricha warned Ravana about Shri Rama's prowess and tried to dissuade him from this endeavor, but Ravana threatened him and forced him to accompany him. Maricha took the form of a golden deer and began wandering around Panchavati. Sita, enchanted by this beautiful deer, requested Shri Rama to capture it and bring it to her. Shri Rama went off in pursuit of the deer and asked Lakshmana to remain there to protect Sita.

When Shri Rama killed the deer deep in the forest, Maricha, while dying, imitated Shri Rama's voice and cried out, 'O Sita, O Lakshmana.' Hearing this, Sita became frightened and urged Lakshmana to go help Shri Rama. Lakshmana initially refused, being certain that no one could harm Shri Rama, but distressed by Sita's harsh words, Lakshmana drew a line and instructed Sita to remain within it, then went in search of Shri Rama.

Taking advantage of this opportunity, Ravana took the form of an ascetic and came to the hut, asking for alms. Sita crossed the Lakshmana line to give him alms, and at that very moment Ravana took his true form and forcibly abducted Sita, placing her in his Pushpaka chariot and flying toward Lanka. Along the way, Jatayu heard Sita's cries and fought a fierce battle with Ravana, destroying the Pushpaka chariot, but eventually Ravana cut off Jatayu's wings with his sword, causing him to fall to the ground. Ravana took Sita to Lanka and kept her in the Ashoka grove, appointing many demonesses to guard her.

When Shri Rama and Lakshmana returned to the hut and did not find Sita, they were deeply shocked. Distraught, they began searching for Sita in the forest. While searching, they encountered the wounded Jatayu, who, with his final breath, told Shri Rama that Ravana had abducted Sita and taken her toward the south. Having said this, Jatayu passed away, and Shri Rama performed his last rites as he would for his father's friend.

Moving further ahead, they encountered a deformed demon named Kabandha, whom Shri Rama and Lakshmana defeated in battle. Before dying, Kabandha revealed that he had been in this form due to a curse and was freed by Shri Rama's touch. He advised Shri Rama to befriend Sugriva, the king of the monkeys, who could help him search for Sita. Kabandha also advised him to visit an ascetic devotee named Shabari.

Shri Rama and Lakshmana reached Shabari's ashram. Shabari, a disciple of the sage Matanga who had long awaited a vision of Shri Rama, welcomed them with devotion and fed them fruits she had gathered through her austerities. Pleased with her devotion, Shri Rama granted her liberation. Then, following Shabari's advice, Shri Rama and Lakshmana proceeded toward Mount Rishyamuka, where Sugriva lived in hiding, fearing his brother Vali. Thus concludes the story of the Aranya Kanda, which describes all the events up to the abduction of Sita.
id_1_4:
On Mount Rishyamuka, Sugriva lived with his four ministers, among whom Hanuman was the foremost. When Sugriva saw Shri Rama and Lakshmana approaching from a distance, he feared that his brother Vali had sent them to kill him. He sent Hanuman to investigate. Hanuman took the form of a brahmin and approached Shri Rama and Lakshmana, asking who they were. Satisfied with Shri Rama's answer, Hanuman revealed his true form and, carrying them on his back, took them to Sugriva.

Sugriva and Shri Rama made a pact of friendship in the presence of fire as witness. Sugriva told Shri Rama his story - how his elder brother Vali, due to a misunderstanding, had driven him out of the kingdom of Kishkindha and had also abducted his wife Ruma. Shri Rama promised Sugriva that he would kill Vali and restore the kingdom to him, and in return Sugriva promised to help search for Sita.

Sugriva told Shri Rama that he had once seen a woman passing through the sky who had thrown down her ornaments while a demon carried her away. He had kept those ornaments safe, and he showed them to Shri Rama. Shri Rama recognized them and understood that they belonged to Sita.

To test Vali's strength, Sugriva asked Shri Rama to kick away the massive skeleton of the demon Dundubhi with just his big toe and to pierce seven sal trees with a single arrow. Shri Rama accomplished both tasks with ease, which gave Sugriva complete faith in Shri Rama's prowess. Sugriva then went to Kishkindha and challenged Vali to battle. A fierce fight broke out between Vali and Sugriva, but since the two brothers looked exactly alike, Shri Rama could not identify Vali and did not shoot his arrow. Sugriva was defeated and returned.

Shri Rama then told Sugriva to wear a garland of flowers around his neck as an identifying mark and sent him to fight Vali again. This time, while the two brothers were fighting, Shri Rama hid behind a tree and shot an arrow at Vali, wounding him. Before dying, Vali questioned Shri Rama about attacking him from hiding, to which Shri Rama explained that, according to the rules of righteousness, Vali had committed a wrong by taking his younger brother's wife, and as the representative of a righteous king, he had the right to deliver justice in this manner. Vali accepted his fault and, entrusting his son Angada to Sugriva's protection, gave up his life.

Sugriva was crowned king of Kishkindha, and Angada was made crown prince. Shri Rama and Lakshmana went to spend the monsoon season on Mount Prasravana, since undertaking battle or travel during the rainy season was considered against scriptural custom. But Sugriva became so absorbed in the joy of gaining the kingdom and reuniting with his wife Ruma that he forgot his promise to search for Sita.

When the monsoon ended and Sugriva made no effort, Shri Rama grew angry and sent Lakshmana to warn Sugriva. Frightened by Lakshmana's anger, Sugriva immediately ordered monkey forces to be sent in search of Sita in all four directions. For the search in the southern direction, Hanuman, Jambavan, and other prominent monkeys were sent under the leadership of Angada, since Sugriva was certain that Ravana must have gone toward the south. Shri Rama gave Hanuman his signet ring, so that Sita would recognize it and trust him.

The monkeys who went south searched for months, but found no success. Eventually they reached the caves of the Vindhya mountains on the seashore, where they met an ascetic woman named Swayamprabha, who showed them the way out of the cave. Coming out, they reached the seashore at the Vindhya mountains, where they realized that the appointed time had run out and there was still no trace of Sita. Fearing failure, Angada and the other monkeys decided to give up their lives there.

At that time, an old vulture named Sampati lived there, who was Jatayu's elder brother. He heard the monkeys' conversation and learned of his brother Jatayu's death. With his divine vision, Sampati saw Sita across the ocean in Lanka in the Ashoka grove and gave the monkeys this information. Sampati also told his own story, of how his wings had burned in an attempt to fly close to the sun, and now, by helping the monkeys, he received the boon of regaining his wings.

With Sampati's information, new enthusiasm arose among the monkeys, but crossing the ocean was a huge challenge, since Lanka lay a hundred yojanas away across the sea. Jambavan reminded Hanuman of his extraordinary powers, which he had forgotten due to a curse received in childhood. With Jambavan's encouragement, Hanuman remembered his own strength, and he resolved to take his gigantic form and cross the ocean from Mount Mahendra to reach Lanka. Thus concludes the story of the Kishkindha Kanda.
id_1_5:
Hanuman took his gigantic form and flew from Mount Mahendra to cross the ocean. Along the way, to test him, the ocean caused Mount Mainaka to rise and offered him rest, but Hanuman politely touched it and continued forward. Then the naga-mother Surasa, to test him, opened her enormous mouth to swallow him, but Hanuman made his body extremely small and passed through her mouth, succeeding in her test through his cleverness. Then a demoness named Simhika caught his shadow to stop him, but Hanuman shrank his body, entered hers, and killed her.

Finally Hanuman reached Lanka. He made his body extremely small and entered Lanka at night. Lankini, a demoness guarding Lanka, tried to stop him, but with a single blow from Hanuman she was knocked unconscious, and she realized that the time for Lanka's destruction, foretold by an ancient prophecy, had arrived.

Hanuman wandered through the magnificent city of Lanka searching for Sita. He entered Ravana's palace and searched through many chambers, and in one chamber, upon seeing the sleeping Mandodari, he mistook her for Sita for a moment, but soon realized his error. Finally he reached the Ashoka grove, where he saw Sita sitting beneath a tree in soiled garments, in a state of deep sorrow and emaciation, surrounded by demonesses standing guard.

At that moment Ravana arrived and again proposed marriage to Sita, along with a threat that if she did not agree, she would be killed. Sita firmly rejected Ravana's proposal and remained steadfast in her devotion to her husband. After Ravana left, a demoness named Trijata, who felt sympathy for Sita, recounted a dream she had that foretold Ravana's destruction and Shri Rama's victory, which frightened the other demonesses.

As the night wore on, Hanuman began slowly narrating Shri Rama's story from the tree, so that Sita would believe he was Shri Rama's messenger. Sita was frightened at first, but Hanuman took his small form, appeared before her, and showed her Shri Rama's ring. Seeing this, Sita was overjoyed and asked Hanuman in detail about Shri Rama and Lakshmana. Hanuman conveyed the message Shri Rama had sent for her and offered to carry her on his back to take her away, but Sita refused, since she wished for Shri Rama himself to come and slay Ravana, who had insulted her. She gave Hanuman her crest-jewel as an identifying token and sent word for Shri Rama to come quickly.

After taking leave of Sita, the thought came to Hanuman's mind that he should test Lanka's strength. He began destroying the trees and fruits of the Ashoka grove. Seeing this, the demonesses informed Ravana, who sent many demon warriors to capture Hanuman, but Hanuman killed them all. Ravana then sent his son Akshayakumara, whom Hanuman also killed. Finally Ravana sent his eldest son Meghanada (Indrajit), who used the Brahmastra to bind Hanuman. Hanuman, to honor the power of the Brahmastra, allowed himself to be bound.

Meghanada brought Hanuman to Ravana's court. Ravana angrily ordered Hanuman's execution, but Vibhishana, Ravana's younger brother who was righteous by nature, explained to Ravana that killing a messenger was against scriptural law. Ravana accepted Vibhishana's counsel and, instead of execution, ordered that Hanuman's tail be set on fire to humiliate him. The demons wrapped cloth around Hanuman's tail, poured oil on it, and set it alight.

But Hanuman shrank his body and freed himself from his bonds, and with his burning tail set fire to the entire city of Lanka. In no time, the whole golden city of Lanka was engulfed in flames. Hanuman then went to the ocean and extinguished his burning tail, and once again went to Sita to confirm her wellbeing. Taking Sita's blessing, Hanuman flew back toward Mount Mahendra.

Having crossed the ocean, Hanuman reached Angada, Jambavan, and the other monkeys, who were waiting for him. Hanuman gave them the joyful news of meeting Sita. Along the way, they stopped at a garden called Madhuvana, where they ate the fruits protected by Sugriva's uncle Dadhimukha and celebrated. They then all reached Kishkindha, where Hanuman gave Sugriva and Shri Rama the news of Sita and her crest-jewel. Shri Rama was overjoyed to hear this news and embraced Hanuman as his beloved friend. Thus concludes the story of the Sundara Kanda.
id_1_6:
After learning of Sita's whereabouts, Shri Rama decided to march to Lanka with the entire monkey army. The vast monkey army, including Sugriva, Angada, Jambavan, Nala, Nila, Hanuman, and other prominent monkey warriors, reached the seashore. At that same time, Vibhishana, who had advised Ravana to return Sita but had been insulted and driven out of Lanka by Ravana, came with his four companions to seek refuge with Shri Rama. Sugriva and some other monkeys expressed doubt, but Shri Rama, following his principle of protecting those who seek refuge, granted Vibhishana asylum and promised to make him king of Lanka in the future.

To cross the ocean, Shri Rama first worshipped the sea god, but when no response came after three days, Shri Rama angrily took up his bow to dry up the ocean. Seeing this, the sea god appeared, asked forgiveness, and suggested a way - that a monkey named Nala, who had been blessed by Vishwakarma, could build a bridge with stones. Under Nala's leadership, the monkey army built a massive bridge over the ocean in five days, over which the entire army crossed toward Lanka.

In Lanka, Ravana began preparations for war. In his court, some ministers advised him to return Sita, but Ravana's pride would not let him accept this counsel. Ravana's brother Kumbhakarna, who remained asleep for six months at a time, was awakened. Kumbhakarna also advised Ravana to return Sita, but eventually, out of loyalty to his brother, he prepared for battle.

The war began. In the first exchange, Angada was sent as an envoy to Ravana, where he gave him a final warning, but Ravana rejected it. Then fierce fighting began. Many demon warriors and monkey warriors clashed with each other. Kumbhakarna entered the battlefield and caused great devastation, but eventually Shri Rama used his divine weapons to cut off Kumbhakarna's limbs and kill him.

After Kumbhakarna's death, Ravana's son Meghanada (Indrajit) entered the battle. Using magical powers, he bound Shri Rama and Lakshmana with the Nagapasha weapon, from which they were freed by the arrival of Garuda. Meghanada then created an illusion of Sita's death to try to break the morale of the monkey army. He then attempted to perform a sacrifice to gain invisible power, but on Vibhishana's advice, Lakshmana disrupted that sacrifice. Finally a fierce battle took place between Lakshmana and Meghanada, in which Lakshmana killed Meghanada.

Grieving and enraged at his son's death, Ravana himself entered the battlefield. During the battle, Ravana severely wounded Lakshmana with a weapon called Shakti. To save Lakshmana's life, on the advice of the physician Sushena, Hanuman went to the Himalayas to fetch the Sanjivani herb. Unable to identify the herb on the mountain, Hanuman lifted the entire mountain and brought it to Lanka, which saved Lakshmana's life.

Then a final, fierce battle took place between Shri Rama and Ravana. Since Ravana had ten heads, no matter how many times Shri Rama cut one off, a new head would regenerate. Finally, on the advice of the sage Agastya, Shri Rama used the Brahmastra to pierce Ravana's heart, killing him. After Ravana's death, Vibhishana performed his final rites, and on Shri Rama's order, Vibhishana was crowned king of Lanka.

Hanuman then went to Sita and gave her the news of Shri Rama's victory. Sita was brought before Shri Rama, but Shri Rama, fearing public opinion and wishing to prove her purity, asked Sita to undergo a trial by fire. Sita entered the fire, and the fire god himself appeared, testifying to Sita's purity and returning her to Shri Rama. At this, the gods too appeared and reminded Shri Rama of his incarnation as Vishnu.

With the fourteen years of exile complete, Shri Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana, along with Sugriva, Vibhishana, and the monkey army, set out for Ayodhya in the Pushpaka chariot. Along the way, they stopped at the ashram of the sage Bharadwaja to receive his blessings. Hanuman was then sent ahead to give the news to Bharata. When Bharata received the news of Shri Rama's return, he was overjoyed and ordered the entire city of Ayodhya to be decorated.

Shri Rama reached Ayodhya, where Bharata lovingly returned the sandals to him and handed over the governance of the kingdom. Under Guru Vashishtha's guidance, Shri Rama's grand coronation was held, and he began his reign as king of Ayodhya. Thus concludes the story of the Yuddha Kanda.
id_1_7:
After Shri Rama's coronation, one day the sage Agastya visited Ayodhya. He told Shri Rama the story of Ravana's lineage and ancestors, including the sage Pulastya, Vishrava, Kubera, and Ravana's birth and the boons he obtained through his penance. He also described how Ravana had conquered Lanka and defeated many gods, gandharvas, and kings through his prowess, including mention of his battle with Vali.

Over time, Shri Rama's righteous and just rule in Ayodhya came to be known as Ramrajya. The people were happy, prosperous, and content. But one day Shri Rama learned that some people in the city were harboring doubts about Sita's long stay in Lanka. A washerman, scolding his wife, said that he was not like Shri Rama, who would take back a wife who had lived in Ravana's house. This remark reached Shri Rama's ears, and considering public opinion to be his duty, in order to uphold his royal responsibility, Shri Rama, with a heavy heart, decided to abandon Sita, even though he had no doubt about her purity.

The pregnant Sita was taken by Lakshmana and left in the forest near the sage Valmiki's ashram. Valmiki gave Sita shelter in his ashram. There, Sita gave birth to twin sons, named Lava and Kusha. Valmiki himself educated both children and taught them to sing the Ramayana.

Years later, when Shri Rama organized an Ashvamedha sacrifice in Ayodhya, Lava and Kusha, now grown into young men, sang the Ramayana at the site of the sacrifice. Hearing their singing, Shri Rama and all those present were astonished. When Shri Rama learned that these two boys were Sita's sons, he requested, through Valmiki, that Sita come forward once again in public to prove her purity.

Sita came to the assembly and declared her complete truthfulness, saying that if she had never, in thought, word, or deed, considered anyone other than Shri Rama, then may Mother Earth take her into herself. With this declaration of truth, the earth split open and Mother Earth herself appeared, taking Sita into her lap and absorbing her into herself. Thus Sita merged into the earth, and Shri Rama was overwhelmed with grief at this final separation from his beloved wife.

Some time later, one day the god of death, Kaladevata, took the form of an ascetic and came to Shri Rama, expressing a wish to speak with him privately, on the condition that whoever interrupted their conversation would be killed. Lakshmana was appointed as gatekeeper. Kaladevata told Shri Rama that the time of his incarnation on earth had come to an end and that he should now return to Vaikuntha.

While this conversation was taking place, the sage Durvasa came to see Shri Rama. Lakshmana refused him entry, but fearing Durvasa's anger and curse, and to protect the entire Raghu dynasty, Lakshmana agreed to sacrifice his own life and opened the door to inform Shri Rama. In keeping with the condition made with Kaladevata, Shri Rama, with a heavy heart, decided to give up Lakshmana, which was as painful to him as death itself. Lakshmana entered the river Sarayu and returned to his divine form as Sheshanaga.

After Lakshmana departed in this way, Shri Rama too understood that his work on earth was now complete. He offered Bharata the kingdom of Ayodhya, but Bharata expressed his wish to go with his brother as well. Finally, Shri Rama entrusted his sons Kusha and Lava with the kingdoms of Kosala and North Kosala respectively, Bharata's sons were given the land of the Gandharvas, and Shatrughna's sons were given the kingdom of Mathura.

Then Shri Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana (who had already departed), and Shatrughna, along with the entire populace of Ayodhya, reached the banks of the river Sarayu. There Shri Rama entered the waters of the Sarayu and gave up his body, returning to Vaikuntha in his original form as Vishnu. Along with him, Bharata and Shatrughna also gave up their lives, and most of the people of Ayodhya, too, entered the Sarayu and gave up their bodies alongside their beloved king. Thus Shri Rama's mission on earth, to slay Ravana and establish righteousness, was fulfilled, and thus concludes the story of the Uttara Kanda and the complete Valmiki Ramayana.
id_2_1:
The great sage Valmiki is known as the Adikavi, the first poet, because he composed the Ramayana, the first epic poem in the Sanskrit language. According to tradition, his earlier life was spent as a bandit named Ratnakara, who robbed travelers passing through the forest to support himself and his family. One day, after a conversation with the sage Narada, self-realization awoke in him, and he began severe penance. It is said that an anthill formed over his body over the years, which in Sanskrit is called valmika, and from this his name Valmiki arose. His ashram was located on the banks of the river Tamasa, where he spent his life in spiritual practice and the pursuit of knowledge.

Sage Valmiki's place in the Ramayana is truly unique, since he is both the author of this epic and also a character within the story itself. When a hunter killed the male of a pair of krauncha birds, and Valmiki was moved by the grief-stricken cries of the female bird, a verse spontaneously arose from his lips, which is considered the first shloka ever composed. By Brahma's grace, he received the complete story of Rama in a vision and composed the Ramayana in twenty-four thousand verses. This text is divided into seven kandas and contains the complete account of Lord Rama's life.

The importance of Valmiki's ashram is also seen in the latter half of the story, where Sita spent her period of exile. After Sita was cast out following the coronation in Ayodhya, she found refuge in Valmiki's ashram. It was here that Sita gave birth to her twin sons, Lava and Kusha, and Valmiki himself educated them and instilled in them proper values. He taught Lava and Kusha to sing the Ramayana, which these two children later performed at Ayodhya's royal court and during the Ashvamedha sacrifice.

Valmiki's life stands as proof that through true penance and repentance, a person can leave their past behind and attain the highest spiritual state. In Indian culture he is worshipped as the Adikavi, and his birthday is celebrated as Valmiki Jayanti. His story teaches us that a person's past is not their identity, but rather their present actions and spiritual practice that lead them to greatness. Thus, sage Valmiki is not merely a poet but stands as a foundational pillar of Indian literature and religion.
id_2_2:
The divine sage Narada is considered a mind-born son of Brahma and has been granted the boon of perpetual travel through the three worlds. Carrying his veena, he wanders through heaven, earth, and the netherworld, and is regarded as a supreme devotee of Lord Narayana. The Puranas describe his birth as arising not from ordinary parents but from the will of the creator Brahma, and for this reason he is also counted among the Prajapatis. He has no fixed dwelling place, since his entire life is spent wandering for the welfare of the world.

Sage Narada's place in Valmiki's Ramayana is extremely important, since the very seed of the entire story of Rama was planted by him. When sage Valmiki asked Narada who, in this age, was a man of virtue, righteousness, and complete excellence, Narada gave a brief account of Lord Shri Rama's life and character. This very conversation became the occasion for the composition of the Ramayana epic, and for this reason Narada is regarded as the first narrator of Rama's story. The brief account he gave was later composed by Valmiki into the extensive text.

Narada appears as an important character not only in the Ramayana but throughout the entire body of Puranic literature. He is regarded as the founder of the path of devotion, and a text called the Narada Bhakti Sutra is attributed to his composition, which explains the nature and importance of devotion to God. He is known as a sage who always speaks the truth and performs deeds for the welfare of the world, though the information he provides sometimes becomes the cause of conflict between gods and demons, always with the underlying purpose of establishing righteousness.

Narada's life teaches us that speaking the truth and spreading righteousness is the greatest service. The message we receive from him is that spreading knowledge and devotion is itself a form of the highest penance. In Indian culture he is remembered with great reverence as the divine sage, and his contribution to the origin of the Ramayana will remain eternal.
id_2_3:
The great sage Vashishtha is counted among the Saptarishis (seven great sages) and was the family preceptor and royal priest of the Ikshvaku dynasty. The Puranas tell that he was born from the radiance of the gods Mitra and Varuna merely at the sight of the celestial nymph Urvashi, and for this reason he is also counted among the mind-born sons of Brahma. His wife's name was Arundhati, considered the ideal among devoted wives, and she is remembered in the form of a star in the sky. Vashishtha's ashram was located near Ayodhya, where he possessed the wish-fulfilling cow Nandini, considered an important instrument of his spiritual practice.

Sage Vashishtha's role in Valmiki's Ramayana is extremely central, since he was King Dasharatha's royal preceptor and bore the responsibility for the education, sacred thread ceremony, and guidance of all four brothers, including Lord Shri Rama. When King Dasharatha wished to perform the Putrakameshti sacrifice to obtain sons, it was under Vashishtha's guidance that this sacrifice was carried out through the sage Rishyashringa. Vashishtha also played a key role in the preparations for Rama's coronation, and later, when Bharata went to the forest to bring Rama back, Vashishtha accompanied him as well.

The conflict between Vashishtha and Vishwamitra is extremely famous in Indian tradition. Vishwamitra, who was a kshatriya king, attempted to obtain Vashishtha's wish-fulfilling cow, but his strength was defeated before the power of Vashishtha's penance. This event inspired Vishwamitra to undertake severe penance to attain the status of Brahmarishi. This conflict illustrates how the power of penance is considered superior to martial strength, and Vashishtha's patience and forgiving nature are distinguishing features of his character.

Sage Vashishtha is also known as the composer of Vedic hymns, and in particular, many hymns of the seventh mandala of the Rigveda are attributed to him. His life provides an excellent example of righteousness, patience, and forgiveness. The life lesson we receive from him is that true greatness lies not in anger or revenge, but in restraint and penance. His tradition as a family preceptor is remembered with respect in Indian culture even today, and his character is considered an ideal example of the guru-disciple relationship.
id_2_4:
The great sage Vishwamitra was originally a kshatriya king named Kaushika, son of King Gadhi. One day, while visiting sage Vashishtha's ashram with his army, Kaushika saw the wondrous power of Vashishtha's wish-fulfilling cow Nandini and attempted to obtain her, but his martial strength was defeated before Vashishtha's power of penance. Inspired by this defeat, he abandoned his kingdom and began severe penance, eventually attaining the status of Brahmarishi, after which he became known as Vishwamitra. His path of penance was filled with many obstacles, including the episode where the celestial nymph Menaka disrupted his penance, from which Shakuntala was born.

Sage Vishwamitra's role in Valmiki's Ramayana is extremely important in the Bala Kanda. When demons such as Tadaka, Subahu, and Maricha were disrupting his sacrifice, he went to King Dasharatha and requested Shri Rama and Lakshmana. Under Vishwamitra's guidance, Rama slew Tadaka and protected the sacrifice. It was Vishwamitra who taught Rama and Lakshmana the mystical powers called Bala and Atibala, which freed them from hunger, thirst, and fatigue, and also gave them knowledge of many divine weapons.

It was sage Vishwamitra who took Rama and Lakshmana to Mithila, to participate in King Janaka's sacrifice. Along the way, he narrated the story of Ahalya's liberation and had Ahalya, who had turned to stone due to sage Gautama's curse, freed by Rama's touch. It was in Mithila, in Vishwamitra's presence, that Rama broke Shiva's bow and married Sita. Throughout this entire sequence of events, Vishwamitra remained central as guide and protector.

Vishwamitra's life is proof that through penance, a person can even transform their inborn nature and rise from a kshatriya to attain the status of Brahmarishi. The life lesson we receive from him is that with firm resolve and unrelenting effort, no goal is unattainable. In Indian culture, his position is also extremely elevated as the seer of the Gayatri mantra, and his character provides an outstanding example of willpower and the power of penance.
id_2_5:
The great sage Agastya was an extremely radiant and diminutive sage, whose birth, according to popular legend, occurred from the radiance of the gods Mitra and Varuna in a pot, and for this reason he is also called Kalashaja or Ghatodbhava. His wife's name was Lopamudra, whom he obtained as a bride from the king of Vidarbha and, through the power of his penance, made into a fitting wife for himself. Sage Agastya's dwelling was located in southern India at the foot of the Vindhya mountains, and according to tradition, it was he who caused the Vindhya mountain to bow down, opening the path for the spread of Aryan culture toward the south.

The story of sage Agastya's extraordinary power tells that he drank the entire water of the ocean in his cupped hands; when the demons Vatapi and Ilvala were deceitfully killing sages, Agastya ate Vatapi as food and digested him, and also killed Ilvala, bringing relief to the community of sages. In Valmiki's Ramayana, sage Agastya is shown dwelling in the Dandaka forest, where Lord Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana visited his ashram during their exile. Sage Agastya welcomed Rama warmly and gave him gifts of divine weapons, including a divine bow, an inexhaustible quiver, and a sword, which proved extremely useful in the war against Ravana in the Yuddha Kanda.

It was sage Agastya who advised Rama to settle in Panchavati, where the abduction of Sita later took place. There is also a story that after Ravana's death in the Yuddha Kanda, sage Agastya taught Rama the Aditya Hridaya Stotra, which inspired Rama to achieve victory in the war against Ravana. Sage Agastya is also considered the seer of many hymns of the Rigveda, and he holds great importance as the founding figure of Tamil literature and culture in South India.

Sage Agastya's life shows that spiritual power and the strength of penance matter far more than physical size. The life lesson we receive from him is that even a small body can accomplish great deeds, if backed by firm resolve and penance. In Indian culture, especially in South India, he is still worshipped with great reverence today.
id_2_6:
The great sage Atri is counted among the Saptarishis, and the Puranas describe his birth as a mind-born son of Brahma. His name comes from a Sanskrit root meaning beyond the three gunas, indicative of his spiritual elevation. His wife's name was Anasuya, renowned throughout the three worlds for her devotion to her husband and her purity. The sons of Atri and Anasuya are considered to be Dattatreya, Durvasa, and Chandrama, of whom Dattatreya is regarded as the combined incarnation of the trinity of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva.

Sage Atri's ashram was located near Mount Chitrakuta in the region of the Dandaka forest, where he performed severe penance for years. Valmiki's Ramayana describes in the Aranya Kanda that during their exile, Lord Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana visited sage Atri's ashram. Sage Atri welcomed all three with great warmth and gave Rama valuable teachings regarding righteousness and conduct. There is also a popular story that through the power of his penance, he was granted a vision of the combined trinity of the gods.

Sage Atri is regarded as the seer of the fifth mandala of the Rigveda, and many Vedic hymns are composed in his name. His life provides an excellent example of simplicity, penance, and the pursuit of knowledge. It was in sage Atri's ashram that Sita received divine garments, ornaments, and teachings on the duties of a devoted wife from Mother Anasuya, which is known as one of the most heartfelt episodes of the Ramayana.

The life lesson we receive from sage Atri is that through penance and the pursuit of knowledge, a person can attain a vision of ultimate truth. In Indian culture he is remembered as one of the stars in the constellation of the Saptarishi, and his character represents the highest tradition of knowledge and self-restraint.
id_2_7:
Mother Anasuya was the devoted wife of the great sage Atri, and her name is spoken with the greatest reverence among devoted wives. Her name itself means free from envy, which represents the greatest characteristic of her nature. The Puranas describe her as the daughter of sage Kardama and Devahuti, and she was married to the great sage Atri. Together with her husband, she established an ashram near Mount Chitrakuta in the Dandaka forest, where her life was spent in penance and righteous conduct.

The story of Mother Anasuya's power as a devoted wife is extremely famous in the Puranas, which tell that once, to test her truthfulness and the power of her penance, the trinity of Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh themselves came to her ashram, and through the power of her penance she received Dattatreya, Durvasa, and Chandrama as her sons. This story is considered proof of her extraordinary purity and devotion to her husband, and her name is invoked in Indian culture as a symbol of ideal womanhood.

The episode of Mother Anasuya in the Aranya Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana is extremely touching. When Sita visited sage Atri's ashram during the exile, Mother Anasuya welcomed her with affection and gave her valuable teachings regarding the duties of a devoted wife. She gave Sita gifts of divine garments, ornaments, and cosmetics, imbued with divine qualities that would never fade. This episode is considered an excellent example of the affectionate relationship between Sita and Mother Anasuya.

The life lesson we receive from Mother Anasuya is that through a life free of envy and devotion to one's husband, a woman too can attain the highest spiritual power. In Indian culture she is counted among the revered women equal to the Panchakanya, and her character continues to provide an ideal example for Indian women even today.

The great sage Bharadwaja is considered a son of Brihaspati, one of the Saptarishis, though some traditions describe him with a different origin. His name comes from the root bharat, meaning to nourish, and he is known as the sage who nourished the knowledge of the Vedas. His ashram was located near Prayaga, at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna rivers, which is still known today as Bharadwaja Ashram and is considered a sacred site for pilgrims.

Sage Bharadwaja's role in Valmiki's Ramayana is extremely important in the Ayodhya Kanda. When Lord Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana left Ayodhya for their exile, they first visited sage Bharadwaja's ashram at Prayaga. Sage Bharadwaja welcomed all three warmly and advised them to settle on Mount Chitrakuta, a beautiful and peaceful region located a short distance from the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna. Following this advice, Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana made their dwelling at Chitrakuta.

Another important episode involving sage Bharadwaja occurs when Bharata was traveling to the forest with a vast army to bring Rama back. Along the way, they too stopped at sage Bharadwaja's ashram, and the sage provided grand hospitality to him and his entire army, including arrangements for divine food and entertainment. This episode is considered an excellent example of sage Bharadwaja's spiritual power and hospitality, and it was through him that Bharata learned of Rama's presence at Chitrakuta.

Sage Bharadwaja is considered the seer of the sixth mandala of the Rigveda, and his important contributions to Ayurveda and grammar are also recognized. The life lesson we receive from him is that hospitality and guidance are also an important part of righteousness. In Indian culture, the Bharadwaja Ashram at Prayaga continues to hold a place of reverence in his memory even today.

The great sage Gautama was an extremely ascetic and renowned sage of ancient India, whose ashram was located in the region near Mithila. His wife's name was Ahalya, whom the Puranas describe as having been created with extraordinary beauty by Brahma's own hands, and it was Brahma himself who arranged her marriage to sage Gautama. Sage Gautama was renowned for his penance and pursuit of knowledge, and his life was spent in Vedic study and the performance of sacrifices.

The most famous story related to sage Gautama is that of Ahalya's curse, described in the Bala Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana. The lord of the gods, Indra, once deceived Ahalya by taking the form of sage Gautama in his absence. When Gautama learned of this, he angrily cursed Ahalya to become a stone, saying that her redemption would come only when, in the Treta Yuga, Lord Rama himself would free her from the curse with the touch of his feet. Along with this, sage Gautama also cursed Indra, causing a thousand marks to appear on his body.

Years later, when sage Vishwamitra was taking Rama and Lakshmana to Mithila, this ashram lay along their path, and Vishwamitra narrated this entire story to Rama. Rama, with the touch of his feet, restored the stone form of Ahalya to her original form, and she was reunited with sage Gautama. This episode is considered an important example of Rama's divine and redemptive nature.

Sage Gautama is also known as the founder of the school of logic (Nyaya), and a text called the Gautama Nyaya Sutra is attributed to his composition, considered the foundation of Indian logic. The life lesson we receive from him is that a balance must be maintained between anger and just decision-making, and that the path of atonement always remains open. In Indian culture, the name of sage Gautama is spoken with reverence as a symbol of knowledge, justice, and penance.

The great sage Jabali was a learned sage of ancient India, considered one of King Dasharatha's royal priests. It is believed his name came from his mother Jabala, which is an example of the practice of the time whereby a child was named after their mother. He had a close relationship with the royal court of Ayodhya, and his knowledge in the fields of logic and materialist philosophy was considered extremely profound.

The most famous episode involving sage Jabali in Valmiki's Ramayana occurs in the Ayodhya Kanda, when Bharata went to Mount Chitrakuta to bring Rama back to Ayodhya. At that time, sage Jabali gave Rama a logical argument that it was inappropriate to honor his father's word and accept exile, since a person has no permanent relationships in this world, and each person is born alone and dies alone. He presented a viewpoint that gave greater importance to political duty and practicality over righteousness, truth, and keeping one's word.

Lord Rama responded to sage Jabali's arguments with great humility but firm resolve, making clear that truth, righteousness, and honoring one's father's word are the true foundation of human life. Influenced by Rama's response, sage Jabali himself clarified that he had presented these arguments only to ease Bharata's grief and to bring Rama back, not as his own actual belief. This dialogue is considered an important example of the philosophical discourse between righteousness and atheistic philosophy.

Sage Jabali's character teaches us that even while listening to various philosophical viewpoints, remaining steadfast on one's own path of righteousness and truth is true strength. This episode is considered a historic instance in Indian philosophy of dialogue between dharma-centered and materialist thought, which further highlights the firmness and righteousness of Rama's character.

The great sage Sharabhanga was an extremely ascetic sage dwelling in the region of the Dandaka forest, whose life was spent in severe penance and renunciation. Detailed genealogical or family information about him is not available in Valmiki's Ramayana, but his character is particularly renowned through his highest spiritual attainment and the event of his ascent to the celestial realm. His ashram was located deep within the dense forests of Dandakaranya, where he remained absorbed in his penance.

The episode of sage Sharabhanga in the Aranya Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana is described in an extremely touching and symbolic manner. When Lord Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana visited his ashram during their exile, sage Sharabhanga was in conversation with the god Indra. Indra had come to invite him to heaven, but sage Sharabhanga said that he would give up his body only after having a vision of Lord Rama. As soon as he had this vision of Rama, sage Sharabhanga kindled a fire through his yogic power and, giving up his body within it, ascended to the divine realm attained through his penance.

Before this event, sage Sharabhanga had expressed a wish to offer his complete power of penance and merit to Rama, but Rama humbly declined to accept it, saying that a sage's fruits of penance should be reserved for his own spiritual elevation. Sage Sharabhanga also advised Rama to go to sage Sutikshna's ashram, which connects to the next part of the story. This episode provides an excellent example of the selfless nature of sages and their boundless devotion to Rama.

Sage Sharabhanga's character teaches us that the ultimate goal of true penance is the vision of the Supreme and the attainment of liberation. The message we receive from him is that after attaining a vision of God, even death becomes like a celebration. In Indian culture, his character is remembered as the highest ideal of renunciation and devotion.
id_2_12:
The great sage Sutikshna was a disciple of the great sage Agastya and performed penance by establishing an ashram in the Dandaka forest region on his guru's instruction. Detailed genealogical or biographical information about him is not particularly available in Valmiki's Ramayana, but his character is presented as an excellent example of devotion to guru and to Rama. His ashram was located in the Dandaka forest, a short distance from sage Sharabhanga's ashram.

The Aranya Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana describes that, on sage Sharabhanga's advice, Lord Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana visited sage Sutikshna's ashram. Sage Sutikshna had been eagerly awaiting a vision of Rama, and when Rama came to his ashram, he embraced Rama with deep emotion. He requested Rama to stay at his ashram and expressed a wish to offer his entire power of penance to Rama, which Rama humbly declined to accept.

Sage Sutikshna advised Rama to go to the ashram of his own guru, sage Agastya, and also showed him the way. In this exchange, sage Sutikshna also spoke of his devotion to his guru and his respect for sage Agastya, which reveals a special feature of his character. Rama stayed one night at his ashram and then proceeded toward sage Agastya's ashram, from which the story continues.

Sage Sutikshna's character teaches us that true devotion should be dedicated not only to God but equally to one's guru. The message we receive from him is that a devotee's heart should be filled with selfless love and dedication. In Indian culture, his character is remembered as an excellent example of the guru-disciple tradition and devotion to God.

The great sage Matanga was an ascetic sage dwelling in the region near Lake Pampa in South India, whose ashram was located in the area around Mount Rishyamuka. According to some traditions, though his birth or caste was not of a high lineage, he attained the status of a sage through the power of his severe penance, which is considered a particularly inspiring aspect of his character. Many disciples performed penance in his ashram, among them a devoted woman named Shabari.

The episode of sage Matanga in Valmiki's Ramayana is described mainly in the context of his ashram and Shabari. Shabari was sage Matanga's most devoted disciple, who dedicated her life to serving her guru. When sage Matanga was about to give up his body and ascend to the divine realm, he blessed Shabari, saying that Lord Rama himself would visit her ashram and grant her liberation. In keeping with this promise, Shabari waited for Rama for years, and finally, in the Kishkindha Kanda, Rama and Lakshmana visited her ashram.

The region of sage Matanga's ashram was considered sacred and divine, and it was believed that due to the power of his penance, even Vali could not enter this region, which allowed Sugriva and his companions to dwell safely on Mount Rishyamuka. In this way, sage Matanga's power of penance is indirectly connected to the episode of friendship between Sugriva and Rama, which became an important event in the Kishkindha Kanda.

Sage Matanga's character teaches us that deeds and penance matter more than birth, and that any person can attain the highest spiritual status through their own practice. The message we receive from him also shows the importance of devotion and loyalty to one's guru, which is made clear through Shabari's character. In Indian culture, the name of sage Matanga is spoken with reverence as a symbol of equality and devotion.

Lord Parashurama was the son of the great sage Jamadagni and Mother Renuka, and is regarded as the sixth incarnation of Lord Vishnu. He was born into the Bhrigu lineage, and his grandfather was the sage Richika and his great-grandfather the sage Bhrigu. Parashurama's original name was Rama, but after performing severe penance to Lord Shiva and receiving from him the parashu, or axe, he became known as Parashurama. His dwelling is believed to have been on Mount Mahendra, where he spent his life in penance and the study of weaponry.

The most famous event of Parashurama's life is the story of his ridding the earth of kshatriyas twenty-one times, which he did to avenge the killing of his father Jamadagni. A king named Sahasrarjuna had killed sage Jamadagni over the wish-fulfilling cow, and in his rage, Parashurama repeatedly destroyed unjust kshatriya kings across the earth. This event is considered proof of his fierce and justice-loving nature, though he later set aside this mission and became absorbed in penance.

Parashurama's episode in Valmiki's Ramayana occurs in the Bala Kanda, when Lord Rama broke Shiva's bow in Mithila and married Sita. Hearing the sound of Shiva's bow breaking, Parashurama, who also possessed the divine bow of Lord Vishnu, came to Mithila in a state of great anger and challenged Rama. With great humility but his own divine prowess, Rama strung an arrow on Parashurama's bow, drawing away his radiance, at which Parashurama realized his mistake and, recognizing in Rama the very incarnation of Lord Vishnu, willingly surrendered his own power.

Parashurama's character teaches us that being fierce for the sake of justice is sometimes necessary, but true strength lies only in the path of humility and righteousness. In Indian culture he is regarded as an immortal incarnation, believed to still be performing penance on earth today, and his character provides an excellent example of mastery in both weaponry and scripture.
